title: Security
intro: Covers who a user is (authentication), what they may do (authorization), the Security Checklist and security policies that harden an application before go-live, and the operator / access group / access role / persona chain behind role-based access control. Questions usually turn on precise distinctions: ARO 'No Access' vs Access Deny, most-permissive role wins, and production-level comparisons.

summary: Authentication establishes who the user is and is the first line of defense. In Pega the operator ID (usually an email address) plus a password is the basic form, and enterprises add single sign-on with SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect or tokens, configured through an authentication service rule. Authorization decides what an authenticated user can do: which data and actions are available at runtime, which rules can be created, read, updated or deleted at design time, and which developer tools such as Tracer are usable.

Pega also separates application-level security, which keeps outsiders out (password rules, authentication, MFA, third-party tools), from feature security, which controls what authorized users can reach (roles for personas, RBAC, ABAC, CBAC). A payroll manager who can see salary data that other HR staff cannot is a feature-security concern. On the record side, the Operator ID record supports authentication, while the access group together with the application supports authorization.
keyFacts: Authentication = who you are; authorization = what you can do.
Authentication is the first line of defense.
SSO options: SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect, tokens; configured via an authentication service rule.
Authorization covers runtime data/actions, design-time rule create/read/update/delete, and developer tools such as Tracer.
Application-level security protects against outsiders (passwords, authentication, MFA, third-party tools).
Feature security governs what authorized users can access (persona roles, RBAC, ABAC, CBAC).
Operator ID record -> authentication; access group + application -> authorization.

rows: Password login, SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect, MFA, authentication service rule
Access roles, ARO, Access Deny, ABAC/CBAC, permission to use Tracer or edit rules

examTraps: MFA and password policies strengthen authentication; they do not grant or restrict features.
Permission to use developer tools or edit rules is authorization, even though it applies to developers.
The Operator ID record alone does not determine what a user can do; the access group does.

objectives.objective: Explain the benefits of the Security Checklist and security policies
summary: The Security Checklist guides a team through hardening an application and is installed as an application guideline rule for each application version. Tasks are grouped by timing (at the start, during development, before deployment) and by area (monitoring, authentication, authorization, auditing, production testing), and the checklist tracks status and completion so security is built in early instead of reworked late. Deployment Manager blocks a production deployment until the checklist is complete, which also supports IT security sign-off. Its four focus areas are data encryption (passwords, properties, BLOBs; sensitive values like SSNs and card numbers), authentication, authorization/access control (RBAC, ABAC, CBAC) and auditing/accountability (failed logins, password changes, rule and data changes). The goals map to the AIC triad: availability, integrity and confidentiality. Security is a shared responsibility of Pega and the client; not every task applies, and Pega Cloud completes some automatically. The most important practices are staying guardrail-compliant and avoiding custom code, which may bypass platform security.

Security policies are configurable controls. Password policy sets length, complexity and predictability rules. CAPTCHA can be the default or custom, shown on initial login or made more likely after failed logins. Lockout, when enabled, uses a failure threshold, an initial penalty in seconds that grows, and a failure log window in minutes; when disabled, a simpler attempts-before-lock and lock-minutes setting applies. Audit policy controls detail captured for login attempts. MFA sends a one-time password by email or SMS that must be used within an allowed time. Operator disablement disables accounts inactive for a set number of days, with an exclusion list. MFA factors are knowledge (password), possession (mobile number) and being (fingerprint); two-factor authentication is a subset of MFA.
keyFacts: Checklist = application guideline rule per application version.
Deployment Manager blocks production deployment until the checklist is complete.
Four areas: data encryption, authentication, authorization/access control, auditing/accountability.
Tasks grouped by timing (start, during, before deployment) and area; status tracked to prevent rework.
AIC triad: Availability, Integrity, Confidentiality.
Shared responsibility; not all tasks required; Pega Cloud handles some automatically.
Top practices: guardrail compliance and avoiding custom code.
Lockout (enabled): threshold, increasing initial penalty in seconds, failure log window in minutes.
Operator disablement: inactive N days, with an exclusion list.
MFA: one-time password by email/SMS within an allowed time; factors knowledge, possession, being; 2FA is a subset.

rows: Default or custom; on initial login; likelihood after failed logins
Enabled: threshold, growing penalty seconds, failure log minutes. Disabled: attempts before lock, lock minutes
Level of detail recorded for login attempts
One-time password via email or SMS within an allowed time
Disable after N inactive days; exclusion list

examTraps: The checklist is not 'all tasks mandatory'; some do not apply and Pega Cloud covers some.
Security is not solely Pega's job on Pega Cloud; it is shared with the client.
Growing penalties after failed logins are Lockout, not CAPTCHA; CAPTCHA only becomes more likely.
Automatically disabling dormant accounts is Operator disablement, not Lockout.

objectives.objective: Describe Operators, Access groups, Access roles and Personas
summary: A persona is the business-facing description of a type of user, managed in App Studio under Users > User management > Personas (the default persona is 'Users'). An access role describes a job function and holds the permissions to perform specific tasks; every persona has an associated role, but not every role has a persona. Creating a persona automatically creates default permissions, a work queue and an access group; creating an access group does not create a persona. Each role has a default channel interface and is associated with studio channels (App, Admin, Dev Studio) and channel interfaces such as a Work Portal.

The operator ID record identifies a person and drives authentication; the access group, together with the application it references, drives authorization. An access group bundles privileges by referencing one or more access roles, which keeps security modular, and several access groups can point at the same application. If an operator's roles conflict, the most permissive permission wins. Users are invited by email and assigned a persona or developer role; generic shared accounts such as 'admin' should not be used. Drafting persona-to-channel associations in the lifecycle does not configure access; by default a persona can reach all pages, and a portal is restricted by assigning personas when the portal is configured.
keyFacts: Persona = business representation; access role = job function with permissions.
Every persona has a role; not every role has a persona.
Creating a persona auto-creates default permissions, a work queue and an access group (not the reverse).
Operator ID -> authentication; access group + application -> authorization.
An access group references one or more roles; several access groups can reference one application.
Conflicting roles: the most permissive permission wins.
Default persona is 'Users'; avoid generic accounts such as admin.
Drafting personas against channels does not restrict access; restrict a portal by assigning personas on it.
Prediction Studio requires the pxPredictionStudio portal in the user's access group.

rows: Links user to an application and one or more roles; supports authorization
Business view of a user type in App Studio; linked to a role

examTraps: Most permissive wins, not most restrictive, when an operator has multiple roles.
Creating an access group in Dev Studio does not create a persona.
Listing a persona for a channel in the lifecycle draft does not limit portal access.

objectives.objective: Configure role-based access control (RBAC) including ARO, Access Deny, Access Manager and production levels
summary: RBAC grants permissions through roles. Pega also supports attribute-based access control (ABAC), which compares attributes of a case, field or document with attributes of the user, and client-based access control (CBAC), which tracks and processes requests to view, update or remove a customer's personal data, as regulations such as GDPR require. Within RBAC, an Access of Role to Object (ARO) holds a role's permissions on a class; 'No Access' denies that permission for that role. An Access Deny rule is an explicit extra layer that blocks access regardless of what other roles grant, which is useful for regulatory requirements.

App Studio's User management landing page (select a persona) is the preferred place to manage access. Dev Studio's Access Manager (Configure > Org & Security > Access Manager) is needed for some permissions, such as deleting a case instance. Best practice is to use these tools instead of editing ARO or Access Deny forms directly. Permissions can be tied to production levels: 5 Production, 4 Staging, 3 QA, 2 Development, 1 Sandbox, 0 deny. Access is granted when the permission's value is greater than or equal to the system's production level. Access Manager only writes 0 or 5, so set other levels by opening the record. For example, a delete permission set to 2 gives full access on a development system (level 2) and no access in production (level 5). Access When rules can add conditions.
keyFacts: ARO = a role's permissions on a class; 'No Access' denies for that role.
Access Deny = explicit deny that overrides grants; extra layer for regulations.
Prefer App Studio User management; Access Manager (Dev Studio) for advanced permissions such as deleting case instances.
Best practice: do not edit ARO/Access Deny forms directly; use the landing page or Access Manager.
Production levels: 5 Production, 4 Staging, 3 QA, 2 Development, 1 Sandbox, 0 deny.
Access granted when permission level >= system production level.
Access Manager writes only 0 or 5; open the record to set intermediate levels.
Access When rules provide conditional access.
ABAC compares object attributes (case, field, document) with user attributes.
CBAC handles requests about customers' personal data (view, update, remove), e.g., GDPR.
examTraps: 'No Access' on one role's ARO can be outweighed by another role (most permissive wins); Access Deny cannot.
The comparison is permission level >= system level; a lower number means fewer environments.
Access Manager is in Dev Studio, not App Studio; it only writes 0 or 5.
Region- or attribute-matching rules are ABAC; personal-data requests are CBAC.

questions.stem: A bank enables a one-time password sent by SMS that users must enter after their password. Which concern does this control address?
options: Authentication, because it confirms who the user is
Authorization, because it limits which features open
Feature security, because it applies to signed-in users
Auditing, because it records each login attempt
questions.explanation: A one-time password is a form of multi-factor authentication, which strengthens proof of identity. Authorization decides what an identified user may do, which an OTP does not change. Feature security governs what authorized users can reach, while MFA is listed under application-level security. The Audit policy records login detail; it does not verify identity.

questions.stem: A security review lists four controls for an HR application. Which two are authorization controls? (Choose Two)
options: Whether a developer may run Tracer in the application
Whether a payroll manager can see salary fields
Requiring sign-in through OpenID Connect
Enforcing password complexity on operator IDs
questions.explanation: Authorization covers what an identified user can do, including use of developer tools such as Tracer and access to specific data such as salaries. OpenID Connect sign-in and password complexity both concern proving who the user is, so they are authentication controls.

questions.stem: Operator jdoe@acme.com signs in successfully but lands in the wrong application with none of the expected case types. Which record should be checked first?
options: The access group and the application it references
The password settings on the operator ID
The authentication service rule
The Lockout security policy
questions.explanation: The sign-in worked, so authentication is fine; what the user can reach is authorization, which comes from the access group together with its application. Password settings, the authentication service rule and the Lockout policy all affect whether a user can sign in, which already succeeded.

questions.stem: A CISO wants MFA and a third-party threat tool to keep outsiders out. HR wants only payroll managers to see salary data. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: MFA and third-party tools are application-level security
Limiting salary data to payroll managers is feature security
ABAC is application-level security since it checks user attributes
Password policies are feature security since only users have passwords
questions.explanation: Application-level security keeps outsiders out with passwords, authentication, MFA and third-party tools. Feature security controls what authorized users can reach, as in the payroll example. ABAC does compare user attributes, but it decides what authorized users can access, so it is feature security. Password policies protect sign-in and are application-level security.

questions.stem: A Deployment Manager pipeline for version 02.01 of an application stops before the production stage. Which is the most likely security-related cause?
options: The Security Checklist for that version is not complete
Some checklist tasks are marked as not applicable
The Lockout policy is disabled
Operator disablement has no exclusion list
questions.explanation: Deployment Manager blocks a production deployment until the Security Checklist is complete. Not every checklist task applies, so tasks that do not apply are expected and do not block anything. The Lockout and Operator disablement settings are security policies, not deployment gates.

questions.stem: A team on Pega Cloud starts using the Security Checklist. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: It is installed as an application guideline rule per application version
Pega Cloud completes some of its tasks automatically
Every task must be completed whatever the deployment platform
On Pega Cloud, security is Pega's responsibility alone
questions.explanation: The checklist is an application guideline rule installed for each application version, and Pega Cloud completes some tasks automatically. Not all tasks are required, so a rule that every task must be done is wrong. Security is shared between Pega and the client, even on Pega Cloud.

questions.stem: After each failed login, users must wait longer before they can try again. Which policy setting meets this?
options: Lockout enabled, with an initial penalty in seconds
CAPTCHA set to appear after failed logins
Lockout disabled, with attempts before lock and lock minutes
Audit policy set to record login attempt detail
questions.explanation: With Lockout enabled, a failure threshold triggers an initial penalty in seconds that grows with further failures. CAPTCHA only becomes more likely after failed logins; it adds no waiting time. The disabled Lockout setting uses a fixed lock time after a number of attempts, not a growing penalty. The Audit policy records detail but does not slow anyone down.

questions.stem: Contractor accounts that have not been used for 90 days must be disabled automatically, except one integration account. Which policy meets this?
options: Operator disablement with an exclusion list
Lockout with a 90-minute failure log window
Password policy with predictability rules
An Access Deny rule on the contractor role
questions.explanation: Operator disablement disables accounts after a set number of inactive days and supports an exclusion list. Lockout reacts to failed logins, not to inactivity. Password predictability rules govern password content. An Access Deny rule blocks permissions for a role; it does not disable accounts, and it cannot exclude a single account.

questions.stem: An architect explains the MFA policy to a client. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: A fingerprint is a 'being' factor
Two-factor authentication is a subset of MFA
A registered mobile number is a knowledge factor
A one-time password stays valid until the next login
questions.explanation: MFA factors are knowledge (a password), possession (a mobile number) and being (a fingerprint), and two-factor authentication is a subset of MFA. A mobile number is a possession factor, not knowledge. The one-time password sent by email or SMS must be used within an allowed time, not at any time before the next login.

questions.stem: A developer creates a new Field Adjuster persona in App Studio. Which two are created automatically? (Choose Two)
options: Default permissions for the persona
A work queue for the persona
A portal that only Field Adjusters can open
A shared generic operator account for testing
questions.explanation: Creating a persona automatically creates default permissions and a work queue. A portal is restricted only when personas are assigned while configuring it, and nothing creates one automatically. Generic shared accounts such as admin are against best practice and are never generated.

questions.stem: An operator's access group lists two access roles. One role's ARO grants Read on the Claim class; the other sets Read to No Access. Can the operator read claims?
options: Yes, because the most permissive permission wins
No, because No Access overrides any grant
No, because the last role listed takes priority
Only if an Access When rule is also added
questions.explanation: When an operator's roles conflict, the most permissive permission wins. No Access on an ARO denies only for that role, which another role can outweigh; an override that blocks regardless of other roles is an Access Deny rule. Role order does not decide the outcome, and no Access When rule is needed because Read is already granted.

questions.stem: During lifecycle drafting, the Manager persona was associated with the Manager Portal. A tester signed in as a Customer can still open the Manager Portal. Which statement explains this?
options: Drafting does not restrict access; assign personas when configuring the portal
The Customer role needs an Access Deny rule on the portal
Manager must be made the application's default persona
Portal limits apply only after the Security Checklist is complete
questions.explanation: Associating personas with channels during drafting does not configure access; by default a persona can reach all pages, and a portal is restricted by assigning personas when it is configured. Access Deny rules block permissions on a class, not portal assignment. The default persona is 'Users' and is unrelated to portal limits. The Security Checklist tracks hardening tasks; it does not turn portal restrictions on.

questions.stem: An SA reviews how personas, roles and access groups relate. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: Every persona has an associated access role
Several access groups can reference the same application
Every access role has an associated persona
Creating an access group in Dev Studio creates a persona
questions.explanation: Each persona is linked to an access role, and multiple access groups can point at one application. The reverse of the first statement is false: not every role has a persona. Creating an access group does not create a persona; it is creating a persona that creates related records.

questions.stem: A role's permission to delete Claim cases is set to 2. The systems are Development (2), QA (3) and Production (5). Where can users with this role delete claims?
options: Development only
QA and Production only
Development, QA and Production
Nowhere, because only 0 or 5 are valid
questions.explanation: Access is granted when the permission value is greater than or equal to the system's production level. A value of 2 meets Development (2) but not QA (3) or Production (5). Reversing the comparison would wrongly grant access in higher environments. Values other than 0 and 5 are valid; Access Manager writes only 0 or 5, but the record can be opened to set another level.

questions.stem: Compliance requires that interns can never update Payment cases, even if another role in their access group grants it. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: Use an Access Deny rule, which blocks access whatever other roles grant
Manage it through Access Manager or the landing page, not the rule forms
Set No Access on the intern role's ARO, which overrides other roles
Edit the Access Deny rule form directly as the preferred practice
questions.explanation: An Access Deny rule is an explicit extra layer that blocks access regardless of other grants, which suits regulatory requirements, and best practice is to manage access through the App Studio landing page or Access Manager. No Access on an ARO does deny for that role, but another role can outweigh it because the most permissive wins. Editing ARO or Access Deny forms directly is not best practice.

questions.stem: A developer wants a role to delete case instances on Staging (4) but not Production (5). Access Manager offers only full access or no access. What should the developer do?
options: Set it in Access Manager, then open the record and set the level to 4
Set level 4 on the App Studio User management landing page
Set the level to 5, which excludes Production
Set the level to 3, since access needs a level at or below the system's
questions.explanation: Deleting case instances is managed in Access Manager, which writes only 0 or 5, so the record must be opened to set an intermediate value; 4 meets Staging (4) but not Production (5). The App Studio landing page is not where this permission is set. A value of 5 grants access in Production too. A value of 3 is below Staging's level, so it would deny Staging, and access requires the permission to be at or above the system level, not below.

questions.stem: A business manager asks that Supervisors be able to permanently delete case instances. Where is this permission configured?
options: Access Manager in Dev Studio
Persona access on App Studio User management
The Security Checklist
The case type's Settings tab
questions.explanation: Some permissions, such as deleting a case instance, can be set only in Dev Studio's Access Manager (Configure > Org & Security > Access Manager). The App Studio User management landing page is preferred for most access but does not cover this permission. The Security Checklist tracks tasks and grants nothing. The case type Settings tab does not hold role permissions.

questions.stem: A lender has two needs: loan officers may open only cases whose Region matches their own Region, and customers can ask for their personal data to be removed under GDPR. Which two access models fit? (Choose Two)
options: ABAC for the Region match
CBAC for the personal data removal requests
CBAC for the Region match, since it compares client attributes
ABAC for personal data requests, since it tracks data subjects
questions.explanation: ABAC compares attributes of a case, field or document with attributes of the user, which is the Region match. CBAC tracks and processes requests to view, update or remove a customer's personal data, as GDPR requires. Swapping the two models gives each need the wrong one: CBAC handles personal-data requests, not attribute matching, and ABAC does not track data requests.
